title: Antidepressants Driving Obesity, Again
subtitle: The vast majority of oral medicines for depression lead to risk of weight gain.
body_html:
The Frontier Psychiatrists is on a tiny crusade. This newsletter wants the world to know that sickness and suffering should can get better. That comes, if one is an adult, with the acknowledgment of risk. As a physician, it's my job to both meaningfully address the problem my patients come to me seeking relief from and be mindful of the risks. One of those risks is weight gain. It's obvious when we're talking about the massive weight gain that we see from second generation and antipsychotic medications, which can be on the order of 2 kg a month for a medicine like olanzapine. However, when it comes to oral antidepressants, for too long, we have downplayed the risks. I've already written about how the use of oral antidepressants in children can lead to being shorter than the child might have otherwise been. The data suggests than antihistamines “for sleep”—those can increase the risk of weight gain, too. I have been on the antidepressants-drive-weight-gain “beat” as a reporter for a while.

Today, we have yet another large data set published in the Annals of Internal Medicine that shines a light on to the pernicious risks of weight gain in oral antidepressants.

Before I dive into that data, let me remind my readers that they all medicines are not the only way to treat depression. In fact, I'm writing this from Kobe, Japan. Why, one might ask, is Dr. Muir in Japan? Does he love expensive beef? No, not at all, I'm actually a pescatarian. I'm here because there's a conference at which I'm presenting some data. It's called Brain Stimulation! It’s very science-y. But at this meeting, a bunch of scientist, many of whom are also practicing physicians, will be sharing data around the role of non-medication treatments for brain disorders. The most commonly treated brain disorder with stimulation of the brain is depression. It's the very same disorder that these oral medication's—I'm bashing—do both less than awesome job treating, and cause adverse effects. We don't have to keep using oral medication's as the only way we can treat brain disorders. We can use brain stimulation instead. We don't have to consider psychiatry a discipline solely for psychopharmacologists. Psychiatry could be a discipline in which people come to a doctor for help with their problems, and the doctor prescribes a treatment. And that treatment? Wait for it. It might not be a pill. It might be something else entirely. It might be a treatment that stimulates the brain, and relieves the depression, and does not include a daily oral medication that causes risk of weight gain, movement disorders, emotional blunting, sexual side effects, and a range of other problems.

We could use brain stimulation as a first line treatment, we could do research about brain stimulation as a first line treatment, we'd have to pay for it though.

But let's take a look at the following data on oral antidepressants, currently considered a first line treatment, and consider, while we're doing it, whether we want this state of affairs to continue. Should people have to take a medication that's gonna make them at risk to gain massive amounts of weight in order to qualify for treatments that are safer, and plausibly more effective? Why do we have to use the unlikely to work treatments with worse side effects first? We don't.

Thank you for joining my rant, or TEDTalk, depending on your perspective.

Medication-Induced Weight Change Across Common Antidepressant Treatments: A Target Trial Emulation Study

This large observational study included 183,118 patients from 8 large US health systems. They pulled data on the prescribing of…

initiation of treatment with sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, duloxetine, or venlafaxine.

They authors started with an assumption:

The investigators estimated the population-level effects of initiating each treatment, relative to sertraline, on mean weight change (primary) and the probability of gaining at least 5% of baseline weight (secondary) 6 months after initiation.

The study was done over two years, but this is looking at pretty short-term weight gain.

They assumed an 8.5lbs weight gain in a 170lbs person in 6 months…compared to being on sertraline. This of course assumes sertraline is some kind of neutral, but mostly it is a way to control for everyone having the same problem enough—it was not comparing not depressed and depressed people. Those we might expect to be different.

What did they find? It is…not good.

Compared with that for sertraline, estimated 6-month weight gain was higher for":

  • escitalopram (difference, 0.41 kg [95% CI, 0.31 to 0.52 kg]),

  • paroxetine (difference, 0.37 kg [CI, 0.20 to 0.54 kg]),

  • duloxetine (difference, 0.34 kg [CI, 0.22 to 0.44 kg]),

  • venlafaxine (difference, 0.17 kg [CI, 0.03 to 0.31 kg]), and

  • citalopram (difference, 0.12 kg [CI, 0.02 to 0.23 kg]);

  • similar for fluoxetine (difference, −0.07 kg [CI, −0.19 to 0.04 kg]);

  • and lower for bupropion (difference, −0.22 kg [CI, −0.33 to −0.12 kg]).

Escitalopram, paroxetine, and duloxetine were associated with 10% to 15% higher risk for gaining at least 5% of baseline weight, whereas bupropion was associated with 15% reduced risk.

People lose weight, bupropion, compared to sertraline, and gain weight on everything else. The risk is substantially higher, to gain at least 5% baseline weight, for Lexapro, Paxil, and Cymbalta.

It's worth remembering that I've already written about how citalopram—the parent compound of the s-enatiomer “escitalopram”—is also the worst drug when it comes to sexual side effects.

Lexapro might be both the worst when it comes to weight gain and the worst when it comes to sexual dysfunction. Awesome. Thank Goodness we have access to these extremely benign drugs. Sarcasm, drip, drip, drip.

Actually, probably thank Goodness unironically. I am grateful that we have access to these relatively safe drugs, because as I remind my readers regularly, depression is a bad illness. Psychiatric illnesses are horrible torture. Many lives have been saved by these medicines. However, many lives have been altered, and ended earlier than they might have been otherwise thanks to the complications of metabolic syndrome, and other problems, thanks to the side effects of these medications. We need to accept the damage we caused as a field, and when better options present themselves, like, for example, non-invasive brain stimulation, we should strive, relentlessly, to bring our patients these better and safer options.

It's really easy to confuse being an advocate for patient with mental illness and being an advocate for the treatments that we have to be aware of for mental illness. These are not the same thing. People talk about pill shaming, and that's not what I'm trying to do here. But even the framing of the term "pill shaming” misses the fact that treatments, other than pills can and should exist. The pills we have, and use most regularly, can and should be of the safer and more effective variety.

We should probably run this entire analysis all over again, using bupropion as the standard, because that's the one that doesn't seem to cause the weight gain.

Keep in mind, there were differences in the study in adherence. Guess what people kept taking? The drug that didn't make you gain a tremendous amount of weight!

Six-month adherence ranged from 28% (duloxetine) to 41% (bupropion).

It's worth mentioning that these variations in appearance did not impact the outcomes of the study, the conclusions remain valid, the confidence intervals just got wider. The study was attempting to enroll individuals who had just been started on an antidepressant, which is more clean statistically, but doesn't capture the burden of weight gain across the population of people who are really struggling with depression. These are first timers, that haven't been said, take a look at the weight change in kilograms:

Now, here is the risk data… this helps us more clearly see that although some people lost weight, and some people gained weight, what really happened is the risk of gaining 5% or more weight was vastly higher in every oral medication other than bupropion, again compared to sertraline, which was the baseline.

Weight gain is not benign. It leads to poor self-esteem, health problems, cardiovascular risk, metabolic syndrome, and early death. It's disabling. You can also be very expensive, because it can lead to subsequent medical problems, or the need for treatment with GLP-1s like semaglutide and tirzepitide.

As a culture, we need to get off this idea that depression is treated with pills, and we just have to ignore, or blame the person, for the subsequent predictable weight gain caused by the complex alterations of biology these medications kick off.

We need to think of depression as an illness that can be treated, and it should be treated, with the most effective treatments that minimize the risk to a person's health.

We've been through this before. We used to casually radiate peoples feet in a shoe store. Until we realize that radiation causes cancer. We can't just use radiation casually. We need to save x-rays for legitimate medical purposes, and not use them on everybody for everything. The same needs to be understood about these oral medications in depression. Depression is a serious illness. We need to learn how to use all of the available effective treatments, and not just by on one class of more dangerous treatment because we've heard of it before.

Thank you for reading. I'm gonna go out and get a walk in Kobe, to combat my risk of obesity. Diet, exercise, and a range of other factors plays a big role in obesity too, I'm told.

And because my daughter is really giving Kawai here, some Quinn-ergy:

I know. I know. One more:

Thanks for indulging me. She is a national treasure no matter where she goes.

Thanks for reading, if you'd like this article, please share with your friends, doctors, health plan, medical directors, fiduciaries at health plans, secretaries of the department of health and human services, and other people in your life, who I imagine, if you enjoy articles like this, probably include some people in senior leadership, determining what we can pay for in healthcare?

I also wrote a book, called Inessential Pharmacology. (amazon link)
